<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par122 />use of ''friend, teacher, servant, neighbour'', either as masculine or feminine; in German, ''Gemahl''<ref>So in early Arabic, ''ba‛l'' (lord) and ''zauǵ'' (conjux) are used both for ''maritus'' and ''uxor''; ''‛arūs'' for ''bridegroom'' and ''bride''; the later language, however, distinguishes the feminine from the masculine in all these cases generally by the ending ''a'' (''at''). In early Arabic also the feminine ending is commonly omitted in such participles as ''ḥāmil, bāṭin'' (gravida), and the like, which from the nature of the case can only be used of females. Thus also {{GHGheb|text=אֹמֵן}}, at least in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=12}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=23}}?), probably means ''nurse'' (for {{GHGheb|text=אֹמֶ֫נֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=4}}, &c.), not ''nursing-father''.</ref> spouse, also for fem. ''Gemahlin'', &c.).

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|g}}
2. Of words denoting persons {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫עַר}} παῖς, according to the formerly common opinion, was in early times used as epicene (see, however, above, {{GHGpar|2|n}}). The use of the plural {{GHGheb|text=נְעָרִים}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=19}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=21}} in the sense of ''young people'' (of both genders) does not, however, prove this. In this and in similar cases (cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=27}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶם}} 32:1) the masculine as ''prior gender'' includes the feminine.<ref>The Arab grammarians call this use of the masculine plural and dual (e.g. ''el-abawāni'', the two fathers, i.e. ''parentes'') ''taghlîb'' or ''the making'' (the masculine) ''prevail'' (over the feminine).—Cf. M. Grünert, ''Die Begriffs-Präponderanz und die Duale a potiori im Altarab.'', Vienna, 1886.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|h}}
'''3.''' The following classes of ideas are usually regarded as feminine,<ref>The masculine gender is attributed ‘by the Hebrews and the Semites generally to whatever is dangerous, savage, courageous, respected, great, strong, powerful ...; the feminine to whatever is motherly, productive, sustaining, nourishing, gentle, weak, ... subject, &c.’ (Albrecht, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1896, p. 120 f.).</ref> although the substantives which express them are mostly without the feminine ending:<ref>When, on the other hand, words ''with'' a feminine-ending, such as {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫שֶׁת|translate=a bow}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=קוש}}), {{GHGheb|text=עֵת|translate=time}} (see the Lexicon), are sometimes construed as masculine, this is owing probably in some cases to a misunderstanding of the formation of the word, the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} of the feminine being regarded as a radical.</ref>

(''a'') Names of ''countries'' and ''towns'', since they are regarded as the mothers<ref>Cf. ''a city and a mother'' ({{GHGheb|text=אֵם}}) ''in Israel'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=19}}. In the same way {{GHGheb|text=אֵם}} (like μήτηρ, ''mater'') on Phoenician coins stands for ''mother-city'', μητ ρόπολις. The same figure is used in such expressions as ''sons of Zion'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=149|verse=2}}; ''sons of Babylon'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=15}}, &c., as also in speaking of the suburbs of a city as its ''daughters'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=45}} ff., &c.—The comparison of Jerusalem to a woman is especially frequent in allegorical descriptions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=1}}, &c.</ref> and nurses of the inhabitants; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַשּׁוּר|translate=Assyria}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱדֹם|translate=Idumaea}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֹר|translate=Tyre}}; cf. also such expressions as {{GHGheb|text=בַּת בָּבֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּת צִיּוֹן|translate=daughter of Babylon, daughter of Zion}}, &c. On the other hand appellatives which are originally masculine, remain so when used as place-names, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית־אֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַגִּלְגָּל}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|i}}
Rem. The same proper nouns, which as names of countries are regarded as feminine, are frequently used also as names of the people, and may then, like national names in other languages, be construed as masculine (the national name almost always being used also as the personal name of the supposed ancestor of the people); thus {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדָה}} masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=8}}, &c., ''Judaei''; but<section end=par122 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
